title: The business of the sommelier
lead: The Certified business column: bottle and pour sizes, the vocabulary, bottle and glass pricing, COGS, the wine list, buying and storing, and selling at the table.

intro.title: THE MATH ON THE EXAM
intro.text: Business of the Sommelier is tested inside the Certified theory exam, with simple math. Examplify has a calculator. These four formulas do most of the work.

sections.name: Bottles, cases and pours

lines.label: Sizes
lines.text: Common: 375 ml (12.7 oz), 750 ml (25.4 oz) and the 1.5 L magnum (50.7 oz). Uncommon: 1 liter, 187 ml and the Jeroboam.

lines.label: Pours
lines.text: Pours per bottle = ounces in the bottle ÷ ounces per pour. The Court's formulas use 25 oz for a 750 ml bottle.

know: A case is 9 liters: twelve 750 ml bottles.
Not every case holds 12: super premium wines can come in 6- or 3-bottle cases.
OWC means Original Wooden Case.
A Jeroboam is 3 L for sparkling wine and 4.5 L for still wine.
Tokaji comes in 500 ml bottles; sake in 300 ml, 720 ml and 1.8 L.

visuals.note: 25 oz ÷ the pour size, using the Court's 25 oz bottle.

sections.name: The words of the trade

lines.label: The list
lines.text: BTG, BTB, pour cost, bottle cost, COGS, cost %, revenue, gross profit, net profit, inventory, spillage, ullage and target cost %.

lines.label: Cost %
lines.text: Cost % is what the wine cost you as a share of what you sold it for. 30% means $30 of product for every $100 of sales.

know: BTG is by the glass; BTB is by the bottle.
Target cost % is the cost % you aim for when you set a price.
Gross profit is the sale price minus the wine's cost. Net profit is what's left after every other expense too.
Ullage is the air space between the wine and the cork.
Inventory change = beginning inventory minus ending inventory.

items.name: BTG / BTB
items.text: By the glass / by the bottle

visuals.title: Wine cost
visuals.text: For every $100 of wine revenue, $30 is what the wine cost.

sections.name: Pricing a bottle

lines.label: The formula
lines.text: List price = bottle cost ÷ target cost %. Check it: cost % = bottle cost ÷ list price.

lines.label: Example
lines.text: A wine costs $20 and you want a 25% cost. $20 ÷ 0.25 = $80 on the list. Gross profit: $80 - $20 = $60.

know: Raise the sale price and margin goes up; lower it and margin goes down.
Raise the product cost and margin goes down; lower it and margin goes up.
Vintage weather changes a Bordeaux's style and its selling price.
Know the current Brunello release and the rough price of top brands.
The Curriculum Guide prints gross profit as cost minus list price; work it as list price minus cost.

items.title: When you…

Pay less for the wine

sections.name: Pricing a glass

lines.label: The Court's formula
lines.text: Glass price = (bottle list price ÷ 25 oz) × the pour. An $80 bottle poured at 5 oz: $80 ÷ 25 × 5 = $16.

lines.label: From cost
lines.text: Cost per pour = bottle cost ÷ pours. Glass price = cost per pour ÷ target cost %.

know: Starting from a case: case cost ÷ bottles in the case = bottle cost.
Bottles needed = (guests × oz per guest) ÷ 25.
Lambrusco by the glass loses its fizz: limited shelf life once open.
Sweet wine by the glass is usually 2 oz; an open bottle lasts about a week cold.
Mix sparkling styles by the glass and bottle to give guests many price points.

visuals.title: Bottles for an event
visuals.text: Guests × ounces per guest, divided by 25 oz, gives the bottles you need.

sections.name: COGS and inventory

lines.label: COGS
lines.text: Cost of goods sold = (beginning inventory + purchases) - ending inventory, all in dollars.

lines.label: Cost %
lines.text: Cost % for the period = COGS ÷ wine sales.

know: Beginning inventory is last month's count; ending inventory is this month's.
Anything that makes ending inventory look bigger makes COGS look smaller.
Wine poured but not charged raises your cost %: cost with no sales.
The theory exam asks about inventory, purchasing, sales and margin situations.

sections.name: The wine list

lines.label: The standard
lines.text: A wine list is clean, correct, current and easy to read. You present it and offer help.

lines.label: On the exam
lines.text: The theory exam includes wine list mistake correction: misspellings, wines in the wrong category and wrong prices.

know: Check producer and region spellings.
Check every wine sits in the right category.
Check prices against your formulas.
Know where each German style and sweetness level belongs on a list.
Sweet and fortified wines by the glass are usually 2 oz; know how long they keep once open.

sections.name: Buying and storing

lines.label: Older wines
lines.text: Before you buy, ask about provenance: who owned it, how it was stored, when it left the winery and how often it changed hands.

lines.label: Storage
lines.text: From Level 1: a constant 50-60°F, cork-finished wines on their side, spirits and fortified wines upright.

know: Inspect older bottles for label damage, leakage and ullage.
Keep wine organized and accessible, away from odors and pests.
Avoid light, vibration, damp, heat, temperature swings and upright storage beyond a few weeks.
Vintage weather changes style and price: know Bordeaux vintages to buy and recommend well.

sections.name: Selling at the table

lines.label: The standard
lines.text: Sales skills are part of proper service. Be ready to talk vintages, style, character, food and quality.

lines.label: Price
lines.text: Find out the host's budget discreetly. If there isn't one, offer several wines at different prices. When in doubt, undersell.

know: Name producer, vintage and full appellation when you recommend.
Explain why a pairing works, in words a guest enjoys.
Keep a short list in your head: crisp whites, full whites, off-dry whites, lighter reds, full reds.
Only recommend producers you know well enough to talk about.
On a price complaint, acknowledge it and state the policy tactfully.

mixups.why: Cost % is a percentage: cost ÷ price. Gross profit is dollars: price - cost.
COGS adds purchases: (beginning + purchases) - ending. Inventory change is just beginning - ending.
A 750 ml bottle holds 25.4 oz. The Court's pricing formulas round it to 25.

facts.fact: Certified learning outcome, Business of the Sommelier: understand pour sizes, wine bottle sizes, define basic business vocabulary, and do basic beverage costing calculations.

Business of the Sommelier is a key pillar of CMS-A education and is tested within the Certified Theory exam. A Certified Sommelier is expected to know basic financial wine program management and costing.
A 30% wine cost means that for every $100 of revenue, $30 is product cost.
Common bottle sizes: half bottle 12.7 oz / 375 ml; standard bottle 25.4 oz / 750 ml; magnum 50.7 oz / 1500 ml / 1.5 liter. Understand how pour size relates to servings per bottle.

Certified column: know common sizes (375 ml, 750 ml, 1.5 liter magnum) and uncommon sizes (1 liter, 187 ml, Jeroboam); calculate ounce or milliliter pours from a standard bottle, e.g. 2, 4, 5, 6 oz or 60, 118, 148, 187 ml.
A Jeroboam is 4.5 liters (six standard bottles) for still wine; in sparkling wine a Jeroboam is 3 liters. A 187.5 ml piccolo or split is typical for a single serving of Champagne.

Terms to know: By The Glass, BTB, Pour Cost, Bottle Cost, Cost Of Goods Sold, Cost %, Revenue, Gross Profit, Net Profit, Inventory, Spillage, Ullage, Target Cost %. Inventory change = beginning inventory minus ending inventory.
A case is 9 liters (twelve 750 ml bottles); not all cases are 12 bottles: super premium wines can come in 6- or 3-bottle cases. OWC means Original Wooden Case.
Sales relation: increasing the sales price increases margin; decreasing it decreases margin; increasing product cost decreases margin; decreasing product cost increases margin.

Formulas: Cost % = Bottle Cost / List Price. List Price = Bottle Cost / Target Cost %. BTG = (Bottle List Price / 25 oz or 750 ml) x oz or ml pour. Pour cost starting from case cost. Bottles needed = (number of guests x oz or ml per guest) / 25.
The Curriculum Guide prints Gross Profit = Bottle Cost - List Price.
Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold; net profit is what remains after all expenses, including operating costs, interest and taxes.
Ullage is the head space between the wine and the cork in a bottle (or the space left in a cask as wine evaporates).
COGS = (BI + P) - EI, where BI is beginning inventory (last month's), P is purchases and EI is ending inventory (this month's), all in dollars or local currency. Cost % = COGS / wine sales.

The theory exam also covers inventory, purchasing, sales and margin analysis, and menu corrections: misspellings of producers or regions, miscategorized or mismatched beverages, and incorrect pricing.
Theory question types include simple business-of-the-sommelier math and wine list mistake correction. A calculator is available on Examplify.
A calculator is available on the Examplify platform; you may bring your own if it has no communication capabilities.
Wine lists are clean, correct, current and easy to read (mise en place). The wine list is presented and assistance offered.

The sommelier is prepared to offer active and appropriate recommendations; sales skills are an essential element of proper service. The sommelier is ready to answer questions on vintages, style, character, food compatibility and quality.
Germany (Certified column): know styles and sweetness levels and where each belongs on a wine list.
World sparkling (Certified column, BOS): the cost of the various sparkling styles and how they fit a well-rounded program by the bottle and by the glass to offer guests many price points.
Lambrusco: limited shelf life of effervescence if pouring by the glass.
Sweet wines: a by-the-glass serving is usually 2 oz; open bottles typically last about a week kept cold in the refrigerator.
Fortified wines: by-the-glass pours are typically 2 oz; know the general shelf life of the wine after opening.
Tokaji bottles are normally 500 ml (17 oz).
Sake bottle sizes: 300 ml, 720 ml, 1.8 L.

Bordeaux (Certified column): yearly weather affects style and selling price; understand Bordeaux vintages and styles to understand price differences, appropriate purchasing and tableside recommendations.
Tuscany (Certified column): know the current release of Brunello di Montalcino and the approximate price of top proprietary brands.

Purchasing older wines: ask about provenance (history of ownership), how the bottles were stored, when they left the winery's cellar, and how many times they've been sold or shipped; inspect for label damage, leakage and ullage.

Storage: constant temperature, 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long term; organized and accessible; away from odors and pests; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified standing up; avoid light, vibration, damp, upright storage over a few weeks, heat and temperature swings.
Discreetly find out if the host has a budget; if not, offer several selections at different price points. When in doubt, undersell: honor the guest's trust on price and perceived value.
Pricing complaints: acknowledge the guest's opinion and tactfully state the restaurant's pricing policy.

Pairing recommendations: say why the pairing works in a guest-friendly way; keep a short mental list of wines for light crisp whites, full-bodied whites, off-dry whites, lighter food-friendly reds and full-bodied reds; name producer, vintage and full appellation for full marks.

The example feedback report scores Appetizing Description and Salesmanship in the service exam, and lists Price & Reputation and Vintage, and Business of the Sommelier: Costing and Program Management, as theory categories.
Know producers if you recommend them at service in the Hospitality and Service Exam (Curriculum Guide).

unverified: The Curriculum Guide prints 'Gross Profit = Bottle Cost - List Price', which gives a negative number. This chapter teaches list price minus bottle cost (the standard definition, Corporate Finance Institute) and says so.
The Curriculum Guide calls (bottle list price ÷ 25) × pour 'BTG Cost'; it gives a glass's share of the bottle's list price, so it's taught here as the glass price.
Jeroboam and 187 ml sizes come from Wine Folly; the Court lists the names without volumes. The Court gives no volume for the 1 liter beyond its name.

Ullage definition comes from the Oxford Companion to Wine on JancisRobinson.com (search snippet; full page not loaded). Net profit definition comes from Corporate Finance Institute. The Court lists both terms without defining them.
Spillage, revenue, pour cost and target cost % are not defined by the Court; the plain definitions here follow from the Court's formulas.
The fortified-wine shelf life after opening is listed as a topic by the Court with no figure; none is given here.
All worked numbers ($20 bottle, $216 case, $12,000 inventory, etc.) are our own examples, not Court figures.

read.bigIdea: Learn the words, and the math gets easy.
read.where: The Curriculum Guide lists the **business vocabulary** a Certified Sommelier must define. Most of it is about cost and price.

stops.name: Selling
stops.text: **BTG** is by the glass, **BTB** by the bottle. **Revenue** is what the sales bring in.

stops.name: Cost
stops.text: **Bottle cost** is what you paid. **Pour cost** is the cost of one pour. **Cost %** = cost ÷ price. **Target cost %** is the cost % you aim for.

stops.name: Profit
stops.text: **Gross profit** is price minus the wine’s cost. **Net profit** is what remains after **all** expenses.

stops.name: Stock
stops.text: **Inventory** is what’s on hand, in dollars. **Spillage** is wine lost in pouring. **Ullage** is the air space between wine and cork.

read.mixup: **Gross profit** subtracts only the wine. **Net profit** subtracts every expense.

read.where: Most Certified math starts with **cost %**. Know the two formulas and you can run any bottle-pricing question either way.

stops.name: Set the price
stops.text: A bottle costs **$20** and your target cost is **25%**. $20 ÷ 0.25 = **$80**.

stops.name: Gross profit
stops.text: $80 - $20 = **$60** on every bottle sold.

stops.name: What moves margin
stops.text: **Raise the price** or **pay less**: margin goes up. **Lower the price** or **pay more**: margin goes down.

read.mixup: **Cost %** is a percentage (cost ÷ price). **Gross profit** is dollars (price - cost).

read.bigIdea: Price the glass from the bottle.
read.where: By-the-glass questions start from either the **bottle’s list price** or its **cost**. The Court’s formulas use a **25 oz** bottle.

stops.name: From the list price
stops.text: **(List price ÷ 25) × pour.** An $80 bottle at a 5 oz pour: $80 ÷ 25 × 5 = **$16**.

stops.name: From a case
stops.text: Case cost ÷ bottles in the case = bottle cost. A **$216** case of 12 = **$18** a bottle. Then carry on as above.

stops.name: For an event
stops.text: **(Guests × oz per guest) ÷ 25.** 40 guests at 5 oz = 200 oz ÷ 25 = **8 bottles**.

read.mixup: A **6-bottle case** changes the math: divide the case cost by 6, not 12.

read.where: From Level 1: COGS = (beginning inventory + purchases) - ending inventory. At Certified you **use** it: run the numbers, and reason through what goes wrong.

stops.name: Count
stops.text: **Beginning inventory** is last month’s count: **$12,000**. **Purchases** this month: **$5,000**. **Ending inventory** now: **$10,000**.

stops.name: What skews it
stops.text: A bigger ending count or missing purchases makes **COGS look lower**. Wine poured but not charged, or sold too cheap, means **less revenue**, so **cost % rises** and margin falls.

read.mixup: **COGS** is dollars of wine used. **Inventory change** is beginning minus ending, without purchases.
